story.title: Oracle sends force majeure notice on its New Mexico Stargate data center

facts.text: Oracle shares fell more than 3% on Thursday following news that the company sent a "force majeure" notice tied to its New Mexico data center project to protect itself from higher expenses.
"Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule," Oracle said in a statement to CNBC.
"We are fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward."
Oracle sent the notice to the developer, which is a unit of Blue Owl Capital , CNBC confirmed.
Blue Owl also saw its shares fall on Thursday.
Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk told analysts on the company's earnings call on Sept.
10 that Project Jupiter would not affect its previously stated fiscal 2027 revenue or earnings guidance.
In a post to X, the company said it remains "committed" to the contract and following the "planned timeline."
— CNBC's Seema Mody and Leslie Picker contributed reporting.
Oracle has sent a force majeure notice to the developer of Project Jupiter, a Stargate data center campus in New Mexico, Bloomberg first reported Thursday.
Force majeure clauses, common in energy and commodities contracts, excuse a party from contractual obligations when events outside its control get in the way.
Oracle is not seeking to exit as the campus’s main tenant, according to Bloomberg’s sources.
Instead, the notice would allow the company to delay payments should the facility miss its 2028 target to come online.
Oracle maintains that it does not expect a delay.
“Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule,” Oracle said in a statement to CNBC .
“We are fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward.”
Project Jupiter is one of the flagship sites of Stargate, the AI infrastructure initiative Oracle, OpenAI, and SoftBank announced with President Donald Trump early in his second term.
The campus has drawn opposition from residents and environmental groups and has become a political flashpoint ahead of the midterm elections.
The notice also comes as AI data center construction faces growing scrutiny nationally, and as developers take on steep costs to build capacity for customers like OpenAI.

Oracle shares dropped about 4% in premarket trading Thursday after Bloomberg News reported the software giant is invoking a "force majeure" clause to shield itself from potential cost overruns on a major data center project in New Mexico.

Project Jupiter covers about 1,400 acres in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, and is one of the sites announced under Stargate, the AI infrastructure venture formed by OpenAI, Oracle, SoftBank and Abu Dhabi's MGX.
Rather than walking away from the project, Oracle is seeking to delay payments if the data center gets derailed and fails to come online in 2028 as planned, according to the report.

The stock decline reflects investor unease over potential friction in Oracle's aggressive data center expansion, a cornerstone of its push to capture growing demand for cloud infrastructure and AI workloads.
Force majeure provisions are typically invoked to release parties from contractual obligations when circumstances beyond their control disrupt performance.
